content.text: {"start": 236.0, "end": 290.0, "segments": [{"start": 236.48, "end": 241.68, "time": "03:56", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "There's also a big loophole in capital gains taxes that the rich exploit called the stepped-up basis."}, {"start": 242.46, "end": 251.42, "time": "04:02", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "If, hypothetically, Warren Buffett were to sell his stock, he'd have to pay capital gains taxes based on his profit, so the cost of the stock minus the original investment."}, {"start": 252.1, "end": 262.64, "time": "04:12", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "But if he holds off selling his entire life, when he dies, whoever inherits the stock and then sells it would only have to pay taxes on what they earned after they inherited it,"}, {"start": 263.52, "end": 266.24, "time": "04:24", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "leaving all those original gains untaxed."}, {"start": 267.2, "end": 273.2, "time": "04:27", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "It's part of what's called buy, borrow, die, and it's one way the richest families avoid paying taxes."}, {"start": 274.02, "end": 283.92, "time": "04:34", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "It's this system and the fact that most taxable capital gains are going to the top 1% that lawmakers see changing the capital gains tax as an easy way to tax the rich."}, {"start": 285.22, "end": 296.72, "time": "04:45", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "President Biden has proposed closing that stepped-up loophole and increasing the maximum tax rate from 20% to 39.6%, but just for people making more than a million dollars a year."}]}

content.text:
John would pay **$4.5 per share (option A)**.

**The rule from the video:** The video explains the "stepped-up basis" [03:56]. If the original owner never sells and dies, whoever inherits the stock and sells it "would only have to pay taxes on what they earned after they inherited it" [04:12–04:24]. The gains made before the death are never taxed [04:24].

**Working it out:**
1. John's basis steps up to the value when Emily died in 2020, which is $150 per share. Her $50 purchase price no longer counts.
2. John's taxable gain is $180 − $150 = $30 per share.
3. The tax is 15% × $30 = **$4.5 per share**.
4. The $100 per share that the stock gained while Emily owned it ($50 → $150) goes untaxed.

The other options don't fit the rule. $19.5 is 15% of the full $130 gain from $50 to $180. $15 is 15% of the $100 gain during Emily's lifetime. $27 is 15% of the whole $180 sale price.

Answer: A
